title: Bad UI Patterns Don't Need Checklists
intro: Baymard published “10 UX Requirements for User-Friendly Carousel Design”. Its first hundred words concede carousels aren't great; the next 2,000 explain how to do them right. That's the problem.

topics.title: Bad UI Patterns Don't Need Checklists

learn.title: A best-practice guide for a bad pattern
learn.text:
Calabro's objection isn't that the advice is wrong. It's that a how-to guide **gives teams cover** to keep using a pattern the evidence says to avoid.

The structure of the article is: “carousels don't work” … “but here's how to make one anyway.”

try.q: What is Calabro's main objection to the Baymard article?
options: It legitimises a pattern the evidence rejects
Its ten requirements contradict the research it cites
It was published without original research
It ignores accessibility entirely
try.explain: A guide to doing it right reads as permission to do it.

left.label: Softened
items: “…but here's how to do it anyway”
Reads as permission to ship it

right.label: Honest
items: If it's harm reduction, say so

learn.title: He grants the counter-arguments
learn.text:
• Everyone uses them anyway, so help make the least-bad version
• It's a stopgap for teams still phasing them out
• Stakeholders insist, and this gives UX folks something concrete
• Reduced harm beats no guidance

He doesn't think any of these is completely wrong. **His point: if harm reduction is the rationale, say so out loud.**

try.q: A team genuinely can't remove its carousel this quarter. What does Calabro ask of guidance written for them?
options: Say plainly that it's harm reduction
Withhold the guidance entirely
Add a disclaimer about the sample sizes behind it
Require sign-off from a researcher
try.explain: He accepts the stopgap; he objects to presenting it as best practice.

learn.title: The bigger pattern
learn.text:
This isn't really about carousels. It's about a trend of **watering down strong evidence** so it feels less confrontational.

We don't want to alienate teams. We want to be helpful. So we offer guidance that makes a bad pattern slightly less bad — and the pattern survives another five years.

try.q: What industry habit does the article criticise?
options: Softening strong evidence to stay agreeable
Publishing usability research without peer review
Relying on competitor analysis
Testing with too few participants
try.explain: Diplomatic dishonesty, in the article's phrase.

test.q: What does the article say about the first hundred words of the Baymard post?
options: They already concede carousels aren't great
They overstate the evidence against carousels
They promise data that never appears
They define the pattern incorrectly
test.explain: Then 2,000 words follow on how to do one anyway.

test.q: Which counter-argument does Calabro accept as reasonable?
options: Stopgap guidance for teams phasing carousels out
Carousels perform acceptably once auto-rotation is off
Carousel performance depends on the industry
Users have learned to expect carousels by now
test.explain: He grants several practical reasons; he wants them stated.

options: Phrasing that softens what the evidence says
Disagreeing privately but agreeing in public
Citing research you haven't read
Avoiding criticism of named companies
test.explain: Such as “don't perform adequately” for “consistently underperform”.

test.q: Why does a how-to guide matter more than an opinion piece here?
options: Teams cite it as permission to ship the pattern
Guides reach a larger audience
Opinion pieces are rarely read by product stakeholders
Guides are harder to correct later

test.q: What is the article ultimately about?
options: How the UX industry communicates evidence
The specific usability of carousels
Baymard's research methodology
E-commerce homepage conversion rates across retailers
test.explain: Carousels are the example, not the subject.
